title: AFB Smears: Red Holds On, a Smear Needs a Crowd
summary: See how the acid-fast stain works, why a negative AFB smear never rules out tuberculosis, and why only specimens from non-sterile sites are decontaminated with NALC–NaOH.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 59 Hit 4 (smear detection limit, sensitivity, specificity), Hit 5 (NALC–NaOH; never decontaminate sterile-site specimens), Hit 17 (acid-fast stain order; fluorochrome alternative), Trap 1 (negative smear) and Trap 2 (decontaminating CSF). Checked against Severova 2025, Aslan 2024, Zaporojan 2024, Mahmud & She 2026, Amrani Souhli 2026. Pending: centrifugation 3,000–3,600 × g and 1.5–2 mL resuspension; heat vs phenol as the mordant; NALC as the mucolytic; the core concept (droplet nuclei) is not taught here.

objectives: Explain the acid-fast stain sequence and why mycobacteria resist decolorization.
Explain why a negative AFB smear does not rule out tuberculosis, using the detection limit of smear vs culture.
Decide which specimens are decontaminated with NALC–NaOH and which go directly to culture.

scenes.title: “No acid-fast bacilli seen” — case closed?
scenes.altText: A sputum cup from a patient with weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss. A slide is stained and read: “No AFB seen.” A clinician token says “TB ruled out?” and a warning mark appears.

cues.text: A patient has had a cough for six weeks, with night sweats and weight loss. Sputum goes to the lab for acid-fast bacilli.
The smear is read: no acid-fast bacilli seen.
Can the lab now say this patient does not have tuberculosis?

scenes.title: Normal: why acid-fast bacilli stay red
scenes.altText: A slide of mixed bacteria. Step 1: carbolfuchsin (red) colours everything. Step 2: acid-alcohol washes the red out of ordinary bacteria, but mycobacteria — with a waxy cell wall rich in mycolic acids — hold it. Step 3: methylene blue counterstains everything that lost the red. Result: red, beaded bacilli on a blue background. A side card: fluorochrome stains (auramine) are read at lower magnification, are faster and more sensitive; the CDC recommends them for primary specimens and carbolfuchsin to confirm isolates.

cues.text: Step one: a strong red dye, carbolfuchsin, stains every bacterium on the slide.
Step two: acid-alcohol. Ordinary bacteria lose the red. Mycobacteria hold it — their waxy wall, rich in mycolic acids, resists the acid-alcohol. That is what acid-fast means.
Step three: methylene blue stains everything that lost the red. So acid-fast bacilli show up red on a blue background.

Many labs screen with a fluorescent stain such as auramine instead. It is read at lower magnification, so it is faster and somewhat more sensitive. The CDC recommends fluorescent stains for patient specimens, and carbolfuchsin to confirm that a culture isolate is acid-fast.

scenes.title: What changes: a smear needs a crowd
scenes.altText: A meter shows bacilli per millilitre of sputum on a log scale. The smear line sits at about 5,000–10,000 bacilli/mL; culture detects about 10–100 bacilli. The patient’s level rises from below the smear line: at low counts the smear is negative even though TB is present. Cards: smear sensitivity is variable (roughly 20–80%); specificity for AFB is high (> 99.9% in one large series); a smear also cannot tell M. tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria.

cues.text: Here is the catch. A smear only turns positive when there are many bacilli — about five to ten thousand per millilitre of sputum.
Culture can detect far fewer — on the order of ten to a hundred. So a patient with TB but a low bacillary load has a negative smear and a positive culture.
That’s why smear sensitivity varies so much, from about twenty to eighty percent. When the smear is positive, though, acid-fast bacilli are very likely really there.
And even a positive smear cannot say which mycobacterium it is. Tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacteria look the same.

props.label: MTB vs NTM? Smear can’t tell

scenes.title: In the lab: decontaminate only what is dirty
scenes.altText: Two lanes. Non-sterile lane: sputum (and urine, stool, gastric) carries normal flora that would overgrow a weeks-long mycobacterial culture, so it goes through NALC–NaOH digestion and decontamination, is diluted, centrifuged, and the sediment is used for smear and culture. A caution: NaOH also lowers mycobacterial viability. Sterile lane: CSF, other normally sterile fluids and aseptically collected tissue skip decontamination and go directly to smear and culture.

cues.text: Specimens from sites with normal flora — sputum, urine, stool, gastric fluid — carry other bacteria. Over weeks of mycobacterial culture, they would overgrow everything.
So the lab digests and decontaminates them with NALC and sodium hydroxide, then dilutes and centrifuges, and uses the sediment for smear and culture.
But sodium hydroxide is harsh. It also kills some mycobacteria, which is why timing is controlled and it’s used only when needed.

Specimens from normally sterile sites — cerebrospinal fluid, other sterile body fluids, and tissue collected aseptically — have no flora to remove. They skip decontamination and go straight to smear and culture.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Negative AFB smear rules out TB” is crossed out → “Smear needs thousands of bacilli/mL; culture and NAAT are the backstops.” Trap card: “Decontaminate the CSF with NALC–NaOH” is crossed out → “Sterile-site specimens go directly to culture.” Trap card: “Positive smear = M. tuberculosis” is crossed out → “AFB could be NTM; identify from culture or NAAT.”

cues.text: Trap one: a negative smear does not rule out tuberculosis. The smear needs thousands of bacilli per millilitre. Culture and nucleic-acid tests are the backstops.
Trap two: never decontaminate a CSF or other sterile-site specimen. Sodium hydroxide kills mycobacteria, and there’s no flora to remove.
Trap three: a positive smear means acid-fast bacilli, not necessarily M. tuberculosis. Nontuberculous mycobacteria are acid-fast too.

scenes.title: Red holds on; dirty gets the lye
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Red holds on” (acid-fast bacilli keep carbolfuchsin through acid-alcohol) and “Dirty gets the lye, sterile goes straight” (only flora-laden specimens get NaOH). A small reminder: “A smear needs a crowd.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: red holds on. Dirty gets the lye; sterile goes straight. And a smear needs a crowd.

Where it breaks: other organisms, such as Nocardia, can be partly acid-fast. Some labs concentrate sterile fluids by centrifugation without decontaminating them. Treatment and drugs like isoniazid can change how bacilli stain. And exact processing steps follow each lab’s procedure.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Acid-fast = keeps carbolfuchsin through acid-alcohol”, “Negative smear ≠ no TB (needs ~5,000–10,000/mL)”, “NALC–NaOH only for non-sterile specimens”.

cues.text: Acid-fast bacilli keep carbolfuchsin through acid-alcohol, but a smear needs thousands of bacilli per millilitre, so a negative smear never rules out TB — and only non-sterile specimens are decontaminated.

explanation.what: Plain language: mycobacteria have a waxy wall that holds a red dye even when acid-alcohol washes it out of other bacteria, but you need a lot of them on a slide to see them. Scientific terms: carbolfuchsin-based (Ziehl–Neelsen, Kinyoun) and fluorochrome (auramine) acid-fast stains rely on mycolic acids and other cell-wall glycolipids; smear microscopy needs about 5,000–10,000 bacilli/mL, whereas culture detects about 10–100.
explanation.why: The lipid-rich wall resists acid-alcohol decolorization. Smear sensitivity depends on bacillary load, so low-burden disease gives smear-negative, culture-positive results. NaOH removes flora that would overgrow weeks-long cultures but also reduces mycobacterial viability, so it is reserved for non-sterile specimens.
explanation.measure: Stain order: carbolfuchsin → acid-alcohol → methylene blue (red AFB on blue). Fluorochrome stains are read at lower magnification and are somewhat more sensitive; the CDC recommends them for primary specimens and carbolfuchsin to confirm isolates as AFB. Smear sensitivity ~20–80%, specificity high (> 99.9% in Mahmud & She 2026). Non-sterile specimens (sputum, urine, stool, gastric) → NALC–NaOH digestion/decontamination, centrifugation, sediment for smear and culture; normally sterile specimens (CSF, sterile fluids, aseptic tissue) → no decontamination.
explanation.differs: Smear (rapid, needs a high load, cannot speciate) vs culture (sensitive, slow) vs NAAT (rapid, sensitive, MTBC-specific); carbolfuchsin vs fluorochrome stains; non-sterile (decontaminate) vs sterile (direct) specimens.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: stain order, why AFB stay red, the 5,000–10,000/mL detection limit, “negative smear does not rule out TB”, and “never decontaminate CSF”.

comparisons.distinguisher: NaOH also kills mycobacteria, so it is used only where flora must be removed.

mnemonic.text: Red holds on. Dirty gets the lye; sterile goes straight. A smear needs a crowd.
mnemonic.explanation: Acid-fast bacilli keep carbolfuchsin through acid-alcohol; only flora-laden specimens get sodium hydroxide (lye); a smear turns positive only with thousands of bacilli per millilitre.
mnemonic.limitation: Other organisms (e.g. Nocardia) can be partly acid-fast; drugs such as isoniazid and treatment can change staining; sterile fluids may still be concentrated by centrifugation; exact processing follows local procedure.

questions.stem: In a carbolfuchsin acid-fast stain, which step separates acid-fast from non-acid-fast organisms?

options.rationale: Correct. Acid-fast organisms resist decolorization by acid-alcohol and stay red; others lose the dye.
Incorrect. The counterstain only colours organisms that have already lost the carbolfuchsin.
Incorrect. The primary stain colours everything; it does not discriminate.
Incorrect. Fixing attaches the specimen to the slide; it does not separate organisms.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary TB has a negative AFB smear on concentrated sputum. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: TB is not ruled out; await culture and consider a NAAT
options.rationale: Correct. Smears need about 5,000–10,000 bacilli/mL; culture detects far fewer, and NAAT is more sensitive than smear.
Incorrect. Smear sensitivity is variable (roughly 20–80%); a negative smear is common in TB.
Incorrect. A negative smear is expected with a low bacillary load and does not by itself indicate a processing error.
Incorrect. A negative smear gives no information about species.

questions.stem: Which specimen should be inoculated for mycobacterial culture WITHOUT NALC–NaOH decontamination?

options.rationale: Correct. CSF is from a normally sterile site; decontamination would only kill mycobacteria.
Incorrect. Sputum carries oral flora and must be decontaminated.
Incorrect. Urine is a non-sterile specimen in practice and is decontaminated.
Incorrect. Stool is heavily colonized and requires decontamination.

references.usedFor: A positive AFB smear requires 5,000–10,000 CFU/mL; culture detects 10–100 CFU from a concentrated sample; sensitivity depends on bacillary count.

references.citation: Zaporojan N, Negrean RA, Hodișan R, et al. Evolution of laboratory diagnosis of tuberculosis. Clin Pract. 2024;14(2):388-416.
references.usedFor: Ziehl–Neelsen identifies acid-alcohol-fast bacteria as red bacilli on a pale blue background (carbol fuchsin and methylene blue); ZN sensitivity 22–80%, needing 10⁴–10⁵ bacilli/mL in one cited range; NALC–NaOH can negatively influence recovery and viability of mycobacteria.

references.citation: Mahmud HA, She RC. Comparison of diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity of Kinyoun and auramine-rhodamine stains in detecting mycobacteria from specimen smears. Microbiol Spectr. 2026;14(7):e0047526.
references.usedFor: Kinyoun (carbolfuchsin with phenol; HCl/alcohol decolorizer) and auramine-rhodamine methods; mycolic acids and cell-wall glycolipids key to acid-fastness; AR detects bacilli more rapidly and sensitively; CDC recommends AR/AO for primary specimens and carbolfuchsin to confirm isolates; specificity > 99.9%, sensitivity 17.4% overall in 16,294 specimens; smears made after digestion/decontamination for non-sterile sources or directly from normally sterile sources; isoniazid and other factors affect staining; non-mycobacterial AFB (e.g. Nocardia, Gordonia) recovered in the series.

references.citation: Amrani Souhli R, Sabri H, Lazraq S, et al. Comparative evaluation of smear microscopy, Xpert MTB/RIF, Löwenstein-Jensen culture, and MGIT 960 for the diagnosis of pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis in Tangier, Morocco. Cureus. 2026;18(5):e109503.
references.usedFor: Sterile body fluids processed without decontamination; non-sterile samples NALC–NaOH decontaminated; CSF processed directly; aseptic tissue inoculated directly; other sterile fluids concentrated by centrifugation alone; Xpert more sensitive than smear; smear cannot distinguish MTBC from NTM.

claims.text: Carbolfuchsin → acid-alcohol → methylene blue; acid-fast organisms resist decolorization (mycolic acids/cell-wall glycolipids) and appear red on blue.
Fluorochrome (auramine) stains are faster and more sensitive; CDC recommends them for primary specimens and carbolfuchsin to confirm isolates.
Smear needs ~5,000–10,000 bacilli/mL; culture detects ~10–100; sensitivity ~20–80%; specificity high.
Smear microscopy cannot distinguish MTBC from NTM.
Non-sterile specimens are digested/decontaminated with NALC–NaOH; NaOH reduces mycobacterial viability; normally sterile specimens (CSF, sterile fluids, aseptic tissue) are not decontaminated.
Centrifuge at 3,000–3,600 × g for 15 min and resuspend sediment in 1.5–2 mL.
claims.note: Not taught; one stool protocol read used 3,000 × g for 15 min with a different resuspension volume.

claims.text: Carbolfuchsin is driven in with heat (Ziehl–Neelsen) or phenol (Kinyoun); NALC acts as the mucolytic.
claims.note: Not taught; the sources read describe the Kinyoun phenol formula but not heat or the mucolytic role.
